title: Build an npv_by_start_year table for a relining

blocks.text: A water utility (invented for this practice) relines old cast-iron mains. A relining job spends `costs[k]` in its `k`-th year of work (`k = 0` is the start year). From the year after the work ends, it avoids `annual_benefit` of break repairs every year, for `life` years. Every amount is quoted in the prices of `valuation_year`, prices rise by `escalation` a year, and the utility's nominal discount rate is `rate`. Amounts are paid at the start of their year. The planning model needs one entry per allowed start year, all valued on the start of `valuation_year`.

Write `npv_by_start_year(costs, annual_benefit, life, starts, valuation_year, rate, escalation)`, returning `{start year: NPV}`. The tests check each entry against numpy-financial's `npv` on the job's year-by-year cash flow, so the conventions above matter.
Write the entry for a start $`t`$ as one formula first: the calendar year of each cost and each benefit, its escalation exponent, and its discount exponent. About twelve lines.

cases.says: at zero rate and zero escalation every start's entry is the life's benefits less the costs
the first benefit arrives in the year after the last year of work, not in the start year
a later start is discounted from the valuation date, so its entry is smaller, as numpy-financial gives it
with escalation, every amount is escalated from the valuation year's prices to the year it is paid, whatever the start

origin.section: Count Benefits to the End of the Asset's Life, Not the End of the Plan

concepts: a coefficient counts benefits over the asset's whole life, past the plan's last year
the coefficient for start t is the NPV of the project's cash flow moved so year k lands in calendar year t + k
